From: Alex Kim <alex.kim@needle.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>

Subject: Proposal: delta-streaming connector for S3 cold-tier

Hi Marissa,

Hope you’re well — quick intro, I’m Alex (partnerships lead at Needle Labs). We build a lightweight delta-streaming layer that ships incremental index diffs from object stores to downstream vector DBs (pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate). Our goal is to make S3-backed cold tiers behave like warm indexes for retrieval-augmented workloads with minimal memory pressure.

High level:
- We tail change manifests written to S3 and emit ordered delta batches (LSN-style) that preserve idempotency and allow replay.
- Clients can subscribe over a persistent gRPC stream or pull incremental files.
- We handle common split/merge tombstones and provide a small on-disk checkpoint for fast resume.

Why we think this matters for Redwood: your hybrid storage routing + cold spillover patterns are a natural fit — customers want low-cost S3 retention but sub-second top-k recall when traffic spikes. We’ve prototyped with small pgvector setups and seen 3–4x improvement in cold-lane recall latency compared to full reindexing.

Would Redwood be open to a co-developed POC? Proposed scope:
- 4-week POC: needle agent deployed in a sandbox S3 bucket + adapter to a pgvector sandbox.
- Success criteria: end-to-end incremental sync with <5s catch-up for daily 10k doc delta, correct tombstone handling, and <10% extra token cost on retrieval path.

I attached a short proposal (needle-delta-proposal.pdf) and can share architecture notes if useful. Can we book 30 minutes next week (Jan 19–21) for a technical sync?

Cheers,
Alex
Partnerships — Needle Labs
needle.ai

Alex — thanks for the note and the proposal. We’re interested in this pattern; it aligns with several customer asks around warm-on-top-of-cold retrieval. A few clarifying questions before we set a tech call: 

1) Throughput & ordering: what steady-state ingest throughput can a single agent handle (docs/sec) and how do you shard across prefixes?
2) Checkpoint semantics: how long do you retain checkpoint state in case of operator reboot? Any operational tradeoffs we should anticipate for multi-tenant Redwood Dedicated pools?
3) Data model mapping: do you expect Needle to emit per-document mutations or shard-level deltas (we ask because pgvector client-side update costs matter in our benchmarks)

If you can answer inline and share any perf benchmarks you have (especially with S3 LIST/HEAD patterns), we’ll loop in infra and propose a concrete POC schedule.

I’ve shared a Drive folder for artifacts: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a2b3c-needle-delta-poc — please upload the arch diagram and any bench CSVs.

—Marissa

Marissa — thanks for the quick reply. Answers below, plus I uploaded the arch diagram and raw bench CSV to the Drive folder.

1) Throughput & ordering: a single agent process on a 4vCPU/8GB host sustains ~1.2k doc/sec for small doc sizes (1–2KB) and about 400–600 doc/sec for large blobs (100–500KB) when using gRPC streaming; we shard by S3 prefix (our recommended default is one agent per prefix shard). Ordering is per-prefix; we surface a monotonically increasing sequence id in each delta batch.

2) Checkpoint semantics: checkpoints are compact (metadata-only) and checkpoint files are retained in S3 for 7 days by default; agents also persist a local checkpoint (rocksdb) that allows resume after short reboots. For Dedicated multi-tenant pools you can run the agent in sidecar mode per customer workspace or centrally with tenant keys — tradeoffs are disk usage and blast radius.

3) Data model mapping: Needle supports both per-document mutation streams (preferred when you need per-doc tombstones) and coarse shard-level batches (good for cheaper throughput). For pgvector we typically recommend per-document deltas when customers expect frequent small updates; that minimizes reindex overhead.

Uploads: delta-arch-diagram.svg, bench-results.csv (summary row + raw samples). Bench highlights: 95th percentile catch-up time for 10k daily delta on a 2-shard setup: 3.8s.

Happy to run a short demo on Thurs Jan 21 at 10am PT if that works.

—Alex

Alex / Marissa — looping in a quick internal take and next steps. Based on the answers and the bench CSV, I’m comfortable greenlighting a limited POC under the following constraints: 

- Duration: 4 weeks starting Feb 1 (we want a week for infra prep).
- Scope: Needle agent in our staging S3 bucket, one pgvector sandbox (single tenant), end-to-end smoke tests for tombstones, and a sequential replay test for 20k docs.
- Success criteria (internal): 1) catch-up latency <6s for the 20k replay, 2) no more than 0.5% index mismatch after a full reconcile pass, 3) documented remediation steps for failure modes (agent crash, S3 eventual consistency).
- Infra ask (Marissa / Vanessa): Redwood will provide a staging S3 bucket, a minimal Dedicated sandbox (2 GPUs) for pgvector, and a service account. Needle provides the agent binary, and a temporary API key.

Action items: 
1) Needle: upload a brief runbook (how to configure prefix shards, how to rotate checkpoint retention) and the Dockerfile/installer.
2) Redwood (Marissa): create staging S3 bucket and share service account creds via our secure vault; schedule kickoff for Feb 1.
3) Alex / Needle: confirm demo time (Thurs Jan 21 10am PT) or suggest an alternative if that’s no longer possible.

Once the runbook is uploaded we’ll open a short Jira epic (VDB-POC-1223) and assign owners. If Needle would like an NDA in place beforehand, share the DocuSign link and we’ll route through Legal.
